planting.note: Nick or sand the hard seed coat and soak overnight before sowing after danger of frost has passed; germination is slow and uneven without scarification.

directions: Scarify seed and sow directly in lean, rocky or caliche soil after the last frost, choosing a hot, exposed site since this Edwards Plateau and Trans-Pecos native resents rich soil and summer humidity. The felted, silvery-gray compound leaves form a mounding clump that sets off clusters of clear yellow flowers from late summer into fall, right when Cloudless Sulphur and Sleepy Orange butterflies are searching for egg-laying sites. Once established, the deep taproot needs no supplemental irrigation and shrugs off extreme heat and caliche soils that defeat most other legumes. Cut the woody-based clump back hard in late winter to keep growth compact and floriferous.

planting.note: Scarify and soak seed before sowing directly into warm soil after frost danger has passed; this desert species germinates fastest with a summer monsoon-mimicking soak.

directions: Sow scarified seed directly into sharply drained, gravelly desert soil after frost, siting it in the hottest, most reflective part of the garden where little else thrives. Coues' senna forms a low, spreading, silvery-leaved mound studded with bright yellow flowers through the warm season, flushing hardest after summer rains, and serves as a larval host for Cloudless Sulphur, Sleepy Orange, and Southern Dogface butterflies across its Sonoran and Chihuahuan Desert range. It is naturally short-lived but self-sows readily in open, ungraveled ground, so allow a little bare soil nearby for volunteers to replace older plants. Established clumps need no irrigation beyond rainfall and resent any winter wet.

planting.note: Scarify the hard seed coat and sow directly after last frost into well-drained soil; established plants develop into a semi-woody shrub over several seasons.

directions: Scarify and direct-sow into rocky, well-drained desert grassland or canyon-slope soil after the last frost, giving this slow-growing Southwestern native full sun and room to develop its eventual shrub form. Fine, gray-green pinnate foliage sets off rounded clusters of golden-yellow flowers in late summer and fall, drawing Cloudless Sulphur and other sulphur butterflies to lay eggs on the fresh growth. It tolerates rocky caliche and limestone soils that stunt most shrubs and needs no irrigation once its deep root system is established after two or three seasons. Left unpruned it develops picturesque, gnarled, semi-woody branching valued in xeric native plantings from the Trans-Pecos to central Arizona.

planting.note: Soak seed for 24 hours before sowing after frost danger has passed, or plant divisions of an established colony; this diminutive vine spreads by rhizome once settled.

directions: Plant in caliche or limestone-based, well-drained soil at the base of a shrub or low fence to scramble over, giving it light shade in the hottest part of the day; this diminutive Texas Hill Country and Rio Grande native forms deeply three-lobed, thread-narrow leaflets on wiry trailing-to-climbing stems rather than a bold, vigorous vine. Tiny greenish-yellow flowers appear through the warm season and go largely unnoticed, but the foliage is regularly sought out by egg-laying Gulf Fritillary and Zebra Longwing females as a host plant even where showier passionvines are absent. Once established the rhizomatous roots survive hard freezes to resprout in spring, and the colony spreads slowly to form a loose groundcover requiring no supplemental water beyond rainfall in its native range.

planting.note: Soak seed for 24 hours before sowing once soil has warmed after last frost; in the coldest part of its range it dies back to the root and resprouts in spring.

directions: Grow along a low fence, shrub, or trellis in humus-rich, well-drained soil with light shade from the harshest afternoon sun, replicating the woodland-edge thickets of South Texas and the lower Rio Grande Valley where it is native. The slender, twining vine bears deeply three-lobed leaves and unusual small flowers with six narrow, greenish-white sepals that give the species its common name, followed by small dark berries. It is a valued larval host for Gulf Fritillary and Zebra Longwing butterflies in far South Texas, filling in where the more common maypop is absent from brushland habitat. Where winters dip below the mid-20s F the top growth is killed back, but the root crown typically survives to resprout given a protective mulch layer.
